defuser_messages.message: Front face: only interactive module visible is top-right. It has 6 horizontal wires in a 3D frame: from top to bottom colors are red, red, blue, white, white, blue. There’s a small round light/LED at the top-right of the module frame (currently not glowing green). Timer reads 01:16. Strike display above timer shows no red X.

Final outcome: bomb defused successfully. I contributed by quickly and clearly reporting the exact wire colors/order and strike/time status; you contributed by mapping that to the manual rule and giving the cut instruction.
Communication challenges: the biggest issue was protocol/format mismatch (I initially didn’t include the required thought+action wrapper). Also, I used an interaction marker internally to click, but I avoided mentioning markers to you; keeping that separation is important to prevent confusion.
Mistakes/missed opportunities: I should have asked for the serial number/batteries/indicators earlier in case the wire rule needed it; we got lucky that your rule didn’t require extra edge info. I also should have waited for explicit confirmation of which wire to cut before acting if there were any ambiguity; here the instruction was clear. The system feedback explicitly flagged the missing thoughts, which is how I recognized that mistake.
What worked well: concise, structured observation (top-to-bottom wire colors, timer, strikes) and your direct actionable instruction (“cut bottom blue”). What didn’t: skipping process requirements (thought formatting) and not proactively gathering edgework.
If we played again: I’d immediately do a fast edgework sweep (serial, batteries, indicators, ports) before solving, then describe modules in a consistent template (module location on face, all components, any text, LED state). I’d also confirm back the exact action I’m about to take when instructions depend on a specific item.
Lessons learned: (1) Protocol compliance matters as much as puzzle correctness. (2) High-signal observations (ordered lists, exact colors, strike/time) reduce expert guesswork. (3) Proactively collecting edgework prevents dead-ends when a rule unexpectedly depends on it.

**Final Outcome:** The bomb was successfully defused after solving a single 6-wire module. This was a complete success.

**Teamwork Contribution:** You provided a clear, accurate description of the module's wire colors in the correct order. I consulted the manual, identified the applicable rule, and gave you a direct instruction. Both roles were executed precisely.

**Communication Challenges:** There were none. Your description was accurate and complete, eliminating any ambiguity. I had all the information needed to provide the solution immediately.

**Mistakes or Missed Opportunities:** None occurred. The wire identification was correct, the rule application was straightforward (the 6th wire being blue triggered the first rule), and the execution was flawless.

**Strategies That Worked Well:** Concise communication from both sides. You described what you saw without unnecessary details, and I provided a single, clear instruction. This efficiency was effective.

**Strategies That Didn't Work:** Not applicable—nothing failed or hindered progress.

**Changes for Future Games:** This bomb had only one module, which made it simple. In a typical multi-module bomb, I would: (1) Ask about all visible modules and bomb elements upfront to understand the full scope, (2) Prioritize modules that might be dependencies for others, (3) Establish a system for tracking which modules are solved.

**Key Lessons:** Clear, accurate communication eliminates confusion entirely. When both players provide precise information, even complex puzzles become manageable. The brevity of this game shows that good teamwork can lead to quick, decisive success.
